title: Java Streams, Lambdas & Modern Java — Revision

sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Java Streams, Lambdas and Modern Java interview questions cover what you need to write idiomatic post-Java-8 code: lambdas and functional interfaces, the Streams API (map/filter/reduce/collect, intermediate vs terminal, lazy evaluation), Optional, and the language features added between Java 9 and 21 (the module system, records, sealed classes, pattern matching, virtual threads, structured concurrency). Interviewers often test whether you actually understand the cost model — when streams help versus when a simple loop is faster — and whether you can spot the bug in a parallel stream. Each answer is structured around the interview-grade insight, not the API reference.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Streams are a **lazy pipeline**: source → 0..N intermediate (map/filter/peek) → 1 terminal (collect/reduce/forEach).

- Intermediate ops are **lazy** — no work until a terminal triggers.
- A stream is **single-use** — re-collecting requires re-creating.
- **Parallel streams** split via the `ForkJoinPool.commonPool` — *do not* use them with side-effecting collectors.

Modern Java additions to remember: **records**, **sealed types**, **pattern matching**, **virtual threads** (Project Loom).

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **Streams are not faster by default** — pipeline overhead can lose to a tight `for` on small inputs.
- **`map` vs `flatMap`** — `flatMap` flattens nested streams; classic mistake on `Optional<Optional<T>>`.
- **`Collectors.toMap`** throws on duplicate keys unless you supply a merge function.
- **Records ≠ JavaBeans** — final fields, no setters; great for DTOs and value objects.
- **Virtual threads** are still threads — but cheap; `Thread.startVirtualThread(...)` and `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"With streams I'd express the transformation declaratively as <map → filter → collect>; the trade-off is readability over a tight loop. For records and pattern matching I'd lean on them where the code is data-shape-driven; for virtual threads I'd reach for them on IO-bound, high-concurrency paths and stay on platform threads for CPU-bound work."*
